## Introduction

In this report we explore a dataset of movies taken from the Internet Movie Database (IMDb). The analysis has three parts: 1. We first load and describe the data 2. We preprocess the data 3. We visualise it.

## The Data

We use the `dplyr` package to manipulate the data and the `ggplot2` package to create plots.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

The data is stored in the file `CleanMovies.csv`, which we load into R.

```{r}
movies <- read.csv("CleanMovies.csv")
head(movies)
```

The dataset contains `r nrow(movies)` films and `r ncol(movies)` variables.

```{r}
nrow(movies) 
ncol(movies)

```

## Pre - processing

Before analysing the data we need to clean it. Some movies in the dataset have a rating of 0, which suggests that they were never rated, and some have a budget or revenue of less than one million dollars, which are unlikely to be reliable. These would distort our results, so we remove them using `filter()`. We also use `mutate()` to create two new variables: the `profit` of each movie (its revenue minus its budget), and the `decade` in which it was released.

```{r}
movies_clean <- movies |>
  filter(rating > 0 , budget >= 1, revenue >= 1) |>
  mutate(
    profit = revenue - budget,
    decade = floor(release_year / 10) * 10
  )
```

This removed 805 movies, leaving us with 8918 movies to analyse. As a check that our new variables make sense, here are the five most profitable movies in the dataset:

```{r}
movies_clean |>
  slice_max(profit, n= 5) |>
  select(title, release_year, budget, revenue, profit) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Visualization

### Movie Ratings

We begin by looking at how the ratings of the movies are distributed.

```{r}
ggplot(movies_clean, aes(x = rating)) +
  geom_histogram(bindwith = 5, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white")+
  labs(title = "Distribution of movie ratings",
       x = "Rating (out of 100)",
       y = "Number of movies")

```

### Genres

Finally, we look at whether some genres are more profitable than others. Each genre is stored in its own `TRUE`/`FALSE` column, so we first use `pivot_longer()` to put them into a single `genre` column, keeping a row for each genre that a movie belongs to (so a movie that is both Action and SciFi appears twice). We then calculate the median profit for each genre.

```{r}
movies_clean |>
tidyr::pivot_longer(Action:SciFi, names_to = "genre", values_to = "in_genre") |>
filter(in_genre == TRUE) |>
group_by(genre) |>
summarise(median_profit = median(profit)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = median_profit, y = reorder(genre, median_profit))) +
geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
labs(
title = "Median profit by genre",
x = "Median profit (millions of dollars)",
y = NULL
)

```


## Conclusion

This report carried out an exploratory analysis of the IMDb movies dataset
